correctness_error_name: Relative-clitic-to-conjunction swap (ש- vs ו-) reverses logical relation
correctness_error_reasoning: The source says 'זוכו ארבעה יהודים מהימין שהואשמו בהסתה' — a relative clause (headed by the bound clitic ש-, Hebrew's equivalent of 'who') that presents the earlier incitement accusation as background to the acquittal: these were people WHO HAD BEEN ACCUSED, and who were now acquitted. The summary renders this as 'זוכו ארבעה יהודים מהימין והואשמו בהסתה' — replacing the relativizer clitic ש- with the conjunction clitic ו- ('and'), which turns the subordinate background clause into a second coordinated main clause. The resulting sentence literally asserts two sequential/parallel events — 'they were acquitted AND [were] accused of incitement' — reversing the presupposed temporal/logical order (charge existed before acquittal) into an ambiguous or backwards one (acquittal, then accusation).
mrl_unique_hebrew_features: Hebrew marks relative clauses with the bound prefix clitic ש- attached directly to the verb, with no separate relative-pronoun word like English 'who/that'. This clitic is phonologically and visually minimal — a single consonant — and is easily confused with the equally minimal coordinating clitic ו- ('and'), also a single bound prefix consonant. Swapping one bound morpheme for the other silently converts subordination into coordination without any other change to the sentence, a confusion that has no analogue in English, where 'who' and 'and' are entirely distinct, non-confusable words.
why_its_factual_error: The claim changes from 'four people who had already been accused of incitement were acquitted [of that charge]' to 'four people were acquitted and [separately/then] accused of incitement' — altering the factual relationship between the accusation and the acquittal (background cause vs. sequential/parallel new event).
evidence_from_summary: זוכו ארבעה יהודים מהימין והואשמו בהסתה, ועניינם היה תלוי ועומד לפני בית המשפט העליון
evidence_from_source_article: זוכו ארבעה יהודים מהימין שהואשמו בהסתה ועניינם היה תלוי ועומד לפני בית המשפט העליון

correctness_error_name: Gender flip of person (grammatical gender reversal of a real party)
correctness_error_reasoning: The source consistently marks the south-wing rights-holder as grammatically/referentially FEMALE using the feminine construct noun 'בעלת הזכויות'/'בעלת האגף הדרומי', feminine possessive suffixes ('שבבעלותה', 'בבעלותה'), feminine verb agreement ('הגישה', 'טענה'), and an explicit feminine independent pronoun ('רשאית היא'). The generative summary systematically converts this same party to grammatically/referentially MALE throughout, using 'בעל האגף הדרומי', the masculine possessive 'שלו' and 'בבעלותו', and masculine verbs ('ביקש', 'פנה', 'טען'). This is not a stylistic variant -- it asserts a different, false fact about who (in terms of person-identity/sex) owns the rights and brought the claim, enabled entirely by Hebrew's grammatical gender marking on nouns, pronouns, verbs and possessive clitics (a system English lacks for this kind of reference). This case is structurally identical to the project's own confirmed severity-5 calibration example (Example A): a consistent source-side feminine referent is flipped to masculine throughout the summary, reversing the factual claim of who (as a person) holds/exercises the right, even though the wing (אגף הדרומי) itself remains identifiable.
mrl_unique_hebrew_features: Hebrew grammatical gender agreement across construct-state nouns (בעלת/בעל), pronouns (היא/הוא), verb conjugation (הגישה/טענה vs. ביקש/פנה/טען), and possessive suffixes/clitics (בבעלותה/שבבעלותה vs. בבעלותו/שלו) -- a feature set with no equivalent ambiguity risk in English, where 'the owner' carries no inherent gender marking that a summarizer could accidentally invert.
why_its_factual_error: The summary asserts that the south-wing rights-holder is male ('בעל האגף הדרומי', 'שלו', 'בבעלותו'), directly contradicting the source, which identifies this party as female throughout ('בעלת הזכויות באגף הדרומי', 'שבבעלותה', 'לשיטתה', 'רשאית היא', 'בבעלותה'). This is a genuine identity/gender fact about a real party to a legal dispute that the summary gets wrong, caused by Hebrew's morphological gender-agreement system rather than by any ambiguity in the underlying facts.

evidence_from_source_article: "לימים הגישה בעלת הזכויות באגף הדרומי בקשה למתן היתר בנייה, לצורך הריסת האגף שבבעלותה... ומשכך הגישה בעלת הזכויות באגף הדרומי תביעה בפני המפקחת על הבתים המשותפים... מנגד, טענה בעלת הזכויות מדרום... לשיטתה... בעלת האגף הדרומי רשאית להגיש את תוכנית החיזוק למוסדות התכנון, ובכפוף לקיום התנאים הקבועים בדין, רשאית היא לבצע הריסה ובנייה, בהתאם לקווי הבניין הקיים הצמודים ליחידות בבעלותה."

correctness_error_reasoning: In the source, the subject of the quoted speech-act sentence is the Mexican visitor Victor ('ויקטור'), referred to by the pronoun 'הוא' two clauses earlier ('ובשבת אחת כשבא איתנו להר הרוח... הוא צימצם עיניים ובין עברית לאנגלית אמר שהצבר של מקסיקו הרבה יותר מרשים'). Hebrew is pro-drop/null-subject-friendly and 'הוא' (he) carries the same masculine gender/number marking as the nearby noun 'הצבר' (the cactus, also grammatically masculine). The summarizer resolved the pronoun 'הוא' to the wrong antecedent, reassigning the verb of speech ('אמר') from the person (Victor) to the plant itself ('הצבר אמר'), producing a sentence where the cactus is claimed to have spoken and compared itself to the Mexican cactus.
mrl_unique_hebrew_features: pro-drop subject pronoun resolution + gender/number syncretism between the pronoun 'הוא' and the nearby masculine noun 'הצבר' (no distinguishing morphological marker separates 'he' the person from 'he/it' the cactus in this local context)
why_its_factual_error: The summary asserts that the cactus plant verbally compared itself to the Mexican cactus variety and found it more impressive -- an impossible, false claim -- whereas in the source it is the human visitor Victor who makes this remark about the Mexican cactus being more impressive than the local one. This reverses who the actor/speaker of the claim is (a person vs. an inanimate plant), which is a genuine factual/identity error, not mere style.
